Leviathan deserves every single negative comment it receives. Every down vote should be doubled. This was a dagger through the heart of an ailing game. A mercy bullet to the head. Over the last few years Paradox has done a sub-par job in producing content for this wonderful community and wonderful game. This patch is a disgrace. 

Here are some reasons why:
** This has been hot fixed as far as I can tell ** - Lag - This game would never lag before, I play on speed 4 and pause all the time. Up until this patch you could scroll across the world as your game ticked away days with no performance issues at all. Your HRE vassal swarm would crawl across Asia into China with no issues at all. Now, you have to pause the game if you want to move your camera lest you want to lag. 4k hours on the same PC and it has never, ever lagged like this before. 

- Pillage Capital - What a massive game breaking mechanic. This mechanic single-handedly has ruined this game for me. It is an interesting concept but in execution it is absolutely terrible. By 1490 as Pegu I had a capitol province of 60 Dev, and I'm sure there are people who had theirs higher. There is a requirement in the Age of Revolutions to have your capitol at 50 dev, this used to mean something. Now everyone can have that done in 40 years from game start instead of being done with 80 years left in the game. By the time I was finished my run I had over 270 dev in my capitol and that was only the mid 1600s. What a joke. North American and Aborigine tribes soar above 50 dev with ease and that's still pre 1500. Was this even tested? How did this mechanic make it through? 

- Favors - Wow.... Just wow... Favors used to be a road block in this game. Let's use my game as Garhwal, an OPM in India, as an example. When I did the 52 Garhs  achievement it was pre Emperor patch, I had to pull a lot of stops to get Jaunpur as an ally and then I had to wait a long, long time for my tiny nation to be able to build up the favors to call in my attack dog. Curry favors has made this an absolute joke. Expanding the favors aspect of the game sounds good on paper, but wow was this ever poorly executed. If you choose to still play this patch then you need to have an ally the entire game as they are just another source of free money and soldiers. In many situations any injection of cash is hard to come by, random events or they cost you a war. Now? just wait until you have 10 favors and every 5 years your get a % of your ally's treasury. You can even take a piece of his manpower pool, one of the most important bottlenecking resources in the early game. 

** This has been hot fixed, file now works ** - Game Breaking Crashes - This is the absolute piece de resistance of this patch. In my current, well now dead, campaign I wanted to use the new broken mechanics of pillage and favors to help me get an achievement I've been after for years, African Power and the Fetishist one to go with it.  Everything is going my way, colonizers are scared of me because its 1545 and I have half of Africa under me and my capitol is massive. I spawned colonialism and this game is just smooth sailing, finally I can get these done. Lo and behold, no I cannot. With my auto save at Sept 1, 1545 that is the end of my run. When I unpause the game it goes until Sept 5th and crashes. Over and over again. I found out that the literal file for the save is full. Just over 100 years from start date the file has no more room and cannot write beyond this date. Incredible.

3. Res Publica - The netherlands and Poland DLC

I undertand how people play the game can change which DLCs are important to them, so everyone wont agree with this list, but for a new player this is what i would recommend.

This is the first review I've written on Steam, and felt compelled based on the overall discussion taking place on the store page. 

Paradox does indeed have an expensive DLC policy, but I will play devil's advocate and defend it (to some extent). 

So many studios crank out games that are quickly, thoughtlessly made, or are carbon copies of their predecessors, put out 1-2 DLCs that add varying degrees of content, then move on to the next thing. That is standard operating procedure, because gamers' attention spans encourage it--we always want the next shiny thing. 

EU4 has kept me interested for years. After 2,000 hours, I have only completed 33% of the achievements, and have many more that I hope to one day pull off (looking at you, Great Khan and This is Persia!). The developers clearly listen to the community when it comes to adding mechanics or adding details and nuance, and despite being 7 years old at this point, they continue to actively add mechanics and flesh out different parts of the world. 

Most companies would have already asked you to by at least one new game at this point, if not two. Developers have to be paid for their work, and Paradox seemingly asks that players who get years of enjoyment on a detailed, well-made game to contribute to its continued development. Considering MMOs often ask you to pay a fee just to use their servers, I don't think it is an unreasonable ask. Granted, certain mechanics from older DLCs that are truly essential to game play (transferring occupation to a subject or ally, supporting independence of subjects, province dev, for instance) should probably be added to the canon at this point for new players to get a faster start, but newer players don't really need Mandate of Heaven or some of the other geo-specific DLCs until they've spent some serious time on the game, and by that point, if they want to go further, then they should also contribute to its development. 

From all I've read, Paradox does a better job of taking care of its developers than many of the big box studios that hire contract designers and lay them off immediately after they've worked them to death. Much like any other industry, paying for "sustainably sourced" content is often a bit higher than buying the discount brands. 

Do I think there should be dozens of unit packs for a couple bucks each? No, and that is where they do milk you for money, but I have never bought one, as it has no bearing on the game's mechanics or playability. A more player-friendly model would be to sell all the unit packs at a slightly higher price, but I have never, ever felt like I missed out on anything by not having them. 

EU4 is the game that moved me from RTS to the hard stuff (pun intended). Most of the Paradox titles I've played are well thought out and stand apart from their competitors (Cities: Skylines, EU4, HOI4, Surviving Mars, and Stellaris, specifically). Anyone strategy fan who wants to be challenged by a game for years to come (and occasionally rage quit and leave it alone for a couple months) should absolutely consider getting the base game with Rights of Man, Art of War, and Common Sense.

After 2000 hours I think it is finally time for a review. This review is about the game as a whole and not just a tiny aspect of it. I will discuss 3 different topics in this review, and they are 1. The game overall 2. The DLC policy 3. A general guide to which of the DLC to get, especially for new players.

1. EU4 is a fantastic game with almost infinite replayability. Don't let the high price tag of the entire game plus all DLC scare you away as only the base game plus one or two expansions are necessary initially, and the rest can be acquired over time as you see fit. Many of the DLC doesn't improve gameplay but is rather cosmetic changes. I still haven't bought one of the expansions. I should add that EU4, like all paradox games, is extremely complex and that this makes the learning curve extreme, however, it is eventually worth it. I would advise newer players to watch a few lets plays to get a better understanding of the underlying mechanics, and it might take a long time to feel like you truly understand the game. Remember that the wiki is your friend. EU4 has some problems and most people think the main ones are the DLC policy and bugs that come with new patches. I cover DLC later and the developer team does actually listen to players and fix bugs and other game breaking elements. Overall I would advise anyone that likes grand strategy games with the time available to get this game, however, unless you are made of money wait for sales because, let's be honest, why wouldn't you. 
This is my actual review of EU4 so if you don't want to read my thoughts on the DLC policy or the specific DLC to get thanks for reading.

2. A ton of people love to hate the DLC policy of Paradox, and EU4 is an excellent example of this policy. However, I do feel that in most cases the complaints are unfair, let me explain why.
EU4 was released in 2013, and the developers are still working on it. There are consistently new features added and changes made that keep the game interesting and engaging and the fact I like many other players have thousands of playing hours proves that it has insane replayability. 
The developers shouldn't have to work for free and releasing DLC is how they are able to work on a game years after release. 
I agree that needed features should not be locked behind a paywall, but I do not think that many truly required features are. Except for a few exceptions which I'll talk about in point 3 I think the DLC are nice to have and not need to have. The reason I can say this is that I played the majority of my game time without many of the DLC, and I am still missing some of it. And, even though there are times that I would like to have a specific feature from a DLC I haven't bought yet I have never been in a situation where I felt that the game was broken because I didn't have a DLC.
Finally, I think most of the DLC actually add enough to the game that they are worth having. I usually get the DLC on sale a short while after it was released and every time I find myself enjoying features that I did not have previously. I think this is exactly what DLC should be, extra content that is fun to have but not essential.

3. If you have made it this far, I applaud you. Here is my opinion on the DLC, I will give each DLC a score out of ten and a short description of when you would want it, I mostly mention the main reason to get it. (I emphasize that this score reflects if you need the DLC and not if it is fun to have. A few are great to have but not initially required. After playing for a while, you will know which you want next)

Going by the date of release:

Conquest of Paradise (only DLC I don't have): 2
Only really necessary for some on that wants to start in North America and a beginner really shouldn't. Also adds random new world that's is really not needed. 

Wealth of Nations: 6
Improves trade and enables trade companies that are currently very strong.

Res Publica: 2
Enables features for merchant and Dutch republics. Only needed if you want to play as one

Art of War: 10
The most important DLC as it improves war significantly (Does other things as well but not as necessary). Get this first. (Almost game-breaking without)

El Dorado: 4
Improves Native American gameplay which is not needed for beginners but also helps colonizers with exploration 

Common Sense: 9
Second most important. Enables developing provinces which give institutions. Good to have when playing in Europe, game-breaking outside Europe 

The Cossacks: 5
Helps with AI interaction, helpful but not needed

Mare Nostrum: 3
Adds Condottieri and map stealing/sharing. 

Rights of Man: 7
Adds tons of things for Monarchies and adds subject interactions. 

Mandate of Heaven: 7
Adds ages mechanics which are fun mid game objectives and improves the Far East which ultimately enhances the game overall.

Third Rome: 1
Only adds stuff to Russia area and Orthodox. Fun if you play there but otherwise completely useless. (This is technically an immersion pack and not an expansion like the other, so unlike the rest, it adds nothing to the rest of the world that I'm just not mentioning)

Cradle of Civilization: 5
Adds tons in the middle east and bit here and there. Not needed for beginners but great for people who play outside Europe

Rule Britannia: 2
Adds features to the British Isles. (Second immersion pack but adds a few minor elements to other nations)

Dharma: 6
Adds a ton to India and a bit to rest of the world especially in regards to their contact with India. Improves governments and policies.

I hope that gives some insight and I want to add that many of the expansions, especially those that were released later, that is not needed initially has tons of great content that adds so much flavor to a fantastic game for players that know what they are doing.

So, Eu4 is a bit of a mixed bag. One of the (if not the) coolest strategy games ever? Check. Insane replayability? Check. Constant updates and free content? Check.

Of course, there's a few downsides as well, such as new mechanics you have to learn and adapt to every patch, a truly massive amount of DLC that's vital to your really being able to play the game, and of course the sometimes variable quality of updates. 

I have over 1800 hours in the game, and I pre-ordered it back in 2013 before it was even released. Why am I only now writing a review? Well, the Paradox community is kind of volatile, and their reactions swing wholeheartedly one way or another with each release and update. Leviathan (the newest update) is absolutely trash and is gamebreaking, but most of the community acts as though Paradox has shanked them in the back and is standing over them laughing evilly. If you're looking to get into EU4 as a new player, just don't buy the Leviathan DLC until they fix this mess and rollback your game to 1.30.6. It really is that easy. EU4 is a fantastic game, and while Paradox's newest studio really dropped the ball with their first ever release, I know it'll get fixed eventually. And if it doesn't, 1.30.6 has all the content I could ever want. EU4 is a fantastic game that has stood and will stand the test of time.

If you are bored of silly AI in strategy games, and look for a deep diplomacy game, you should definitely play this game.

You are probably wondering why I would give this game a negative review.  In essence, I am not.  This is one of the most satisfying gaming experiences of my entire life.  The depth at which this game takes you into grand strategy gaming is incredible.  There isn't much more to say to that point which hasn't already been said above and below.

Where is the problem then?

The answer is easy and I am guessing you already know it.   DLC and price gouging.  DLC among all games is an annoying issue we will probably never rid ourselves of.  That ship has sailed.  However, this game specifically, is by far one of the most obvious offenders.  

We can argue over supply and demand.  We can argue over worth and value.  We can also say that you don't have to buy the DLC to enjoy the game.  In many ways I can see both sides of the argument. I do not own a game development studio and I do not know how to make a video game.  Yet, I find it hard to believe that some of this DLC can't be more affordable.  If you are one of those players who bought this game at its inception and bought every DLC as it came out, the burden is less of an impact.  Now imagine you are buying the game for the first time.  Who in their right mind would want to pay $263.93 for a game?  And that isn't including all the other things that are available for this game.

I am one of those players who just doesn't like playing an incomplete game. I feel like most gamers, who would be interested in this game, are of a like mind to that sentiment.  We wanted detail and a very immersive experience.  That is why we love this game.  Is it possible that the developers are aware of our "fixation" and are maliciously taking advantage of us?  I would also gamble that the players of this game have a higher average income to those players of other games.  Is that something they also are exploiting?  I can get real conspiratorial when you are asking me to spend close to $300 for a complete game.

This game is unique in that some DLC might not even have an impact on your game based on your starting position, government, culture, etc., etc.  Would you then argue to me that I should not have purchased the DLC?  I would argue the butterfly effect.  It might not be obvious on its face, but a change has been made.  And this argument hasn't even started on the quality of some DLC...which also might not be seen on its face.  

I am just a small voice here.  I am not very confident that my chirping will get much traction or be seen by anyone influential enough to make a difference.  I do like this game.  You should buy it.  Just be warned that this is like a cocaine habit.  Not as bad as Magic: The Gathering, but a top contender for money sucks.

I'm a working professional with kids/wife/mortgage and this review is written for folks in similar situations. 

This is the best grand-strategy game that I have ever played. It's polished, deep, addictive, beautiful, and immensely fun especially if you are a fan of European history. EU4 is one of the few games with a long solo campaign that I could play a handful of hours every week (more on the weekends) over several years and still enjoy multiple campaigns.

Regarding the DLC strategy used by Paradox that many reviewers rail against; I have spent at least $150 over the last 4-years for the base game and DLC, often during sales, and it was worth every penny for the 1000+ hours of gameplay. DLC sales keep the programmers employed (looking at you DDRJake) and ensure that this game keeps getting more polish and features. Paradox is a business, not a charity, and they need to get paid if we want to keep getting great content. I'm not a college student on a limited budget (I was once), but simple math shows me that I enjoyed 1,100 hours at a cost of around $0.13/hour, and that is cheap entertainment.

Here are some tips for beginners or people interested in trying the solo game: 

1) Don't play the demo. It's completely out of date.

2) Watch Quill18 or Arumba's Let's Plays on youtube to learn the game and figure out if you like it before buying. If all the map modes and menu screens don't look like fun, then stay away. The 2-hour trial period for a full refund from Steam is not enough time to learn the game and you will be frustrated and hate it. When you buy it, you'll need to commit to a lot of DLC to make the game enjoyable and at least 20+ hours over several days to learn the mechanics.

3) Start your first game as Castille. They are rich, powerful, and stable, and have good opportunities for expansion in Iberia and North Africa. Poland is another good beginner start. Austria/France are for novice players. England/Sweden are for players with a more advanced understanding of game mechanics. Italian states, Japanese Daymo, and Brandenburg will be almost impossible (and boring) for beginners, so leave these for later campaigns as they are very enjoyable nations once you understand all game mechanics. Stay away from Byzantium. Just stay away.

4) This is not Total War and battles can't be micromanaged at a regimental level. When possible, give your general advantages by choosing favorable locations for engagements, such as mountains, or areas where the enemy must cross a river to reach you.

5) Retreat is sometimes necessary. Don't sacrifice your men for the sake of honor.

6) As in real life, the victors in EU4's wars usually have superior troop quantity and/or quality. This is one of the only games I can think of where you can win almost all of the battles by using superior troops and still lose the war by running out of men due to attrition and casualties. Russian winters can really decimate your Prussian "space marines" and massive Chinese armies can stall your Spanish colonial expansion plans on the Asian mainland for a century. Choose the timing of your wars carefully.

7) The AI will eventually give you a bloody nose in the form of a coalition war or a surprise attack when you are already fighting several other wars. Don't quit in frustration; learn from your mistakes. I still got surprised a few times after 1000+ hours of play and you will, too.

8) Don't fear going into debt if you are fighting a long bloody war or get a great random event that requires cash.

9) Don't trust the French and don't underestimate the danger in letting them expand out of control. Drown them in the bodies of loyal allies and mercenaries if you must.

10) Choose monarch points over money. Always.

Thanks for reading!

I love the Paradox games.
I haven't missed a single one of their in-house developments since Hearts of Iron 3 got me hooked on Grand Strategy.
As a history nerd, I adore the image of history they portray - that everything could be totally different, that history isn't a traintrack without forks - and as a gamer who loves being able to not only play good guys, it's great fun to paint the globe in your color.

Europa Universalis 4 is no exception here. It's a great game with tons of replayability that can offer you countless hours of fun, if you are willing to learn the game (which has become a lot easier since previous iterations) and are enjoying this mix of "warfare management" (where you only command the armies and thus the overall strategy, not the tactics of individual units) and empire management.
So, for that, I would give this game a resounding recommendation.

However, I still cannot give this game a thumbs-up and overall recommendation for a very simple reason:
Paradox's DLC policy for EU4.

For a lot of games, Paradox has a fairly fair policy: They offer many, many DLCs at relatively low price that contain visual changes (so, if you wanna make the armies look even more authentic and/or cool, you buy them, if you think it's worth the extra bucks) and a few expansions at slightly higher price points that add a couple of extra features. However, most of these features are fully optional and they are usually accompanied by free updates that improve the game, so expansions are nice to have but not mandatory.
The DLC policy they have for Crusader Kings 2 or Hearts of Iron 4 follows that model and I have no objections to that.

For EU4, however, it feels different.
There have been six expansions for EU4, with the seventh (Dharma) to be released in a few days as of the writing of this review, and several of these expansions have mixed reviews. Some of them add several new features, some of them just focus on changing a few things around in certain areas of the world (or for certain countries) without bringing too much substantial to the table - yet the price for all of these expansions is set at 20€ or your regional equivalent. That puts the overall price for the game, with all expansions, currently at around 150€.

Now, that might not be something to be too disappointed with and affect the recommendation like that (though I would argue that it is kinda ridiculous to pay as much for a 'complete' game as you would for a new console, regardless of whether that game is EU4, Fallout 4 or any of the Call of Duties).
But the thing is: Some of their features arguably should have been part of the free updates because they are such immense quality of life improvements (like, for example, being able to switch out the occupants of a province, which is absolutely essential for distributing the spoils of war and the fact that it is not part of the base game can result in situations that require save-scumming to get around them when you are fighting in a war with an ally who keeps occupying territory that you want to claim - or vice versa, where you occupied territory you want to give to your ally but have to let your enemy reconquer so your ally can occupy again, just so you can give it to your ally in the peace deal).

It's the combination of these three factors (an arguably too high price point, some expansions with too few features to justify their price, and some features that seem so critical that it feels a little like coercion to lock them behind a 20€ paywall) that leads me to recommend Europa Universalis 4 in principle but I still cannot give it an 'official' recommendation due to the DLC policy that is, in my opinion, the worst of any Paradox game.

I would not recommend buying any DLC for this game unless there is a substantial (50% and more) discount, and I urge Paradox to overthink this kind of DLC policy - if not for EU4, then for their next release, because a lapse in judgement is one thing, selling overpriced products another.

As a seasoned player and enthusiast of the grand strategy genre, Europa Universalis IV (EU4) is hands down my favorite game. It offers a depth and complexity that is unparalleled in the strategy game market and allows me to experience history in a way that no other game can.

One of the things that I love about EU4 is the sheer scale of the game. The game spans from the late Middle Ages to the early modern period, and allows you to play as any of the nearly 500 different nations in the game. Each nation has its own unique attributes and challenges, making each playthrough a completely different experience.

Another standout feature of EU4 is its focus on historical accuracy. The game models everything from the political alliances of the time to the technological advancements of each nation, giving players a sense of immersion that is hard to match in any other game. I love how the game allows me to explore different historical what-if scenarios, such as what would happen if the Ottoman Empire conquered Europe or if France was never defeated in the Hundred Years' War.

The game also has a steep learning curve, which I see as a positive. It takes time and effort to master the intricacies of the game, but once you do, the sense of satisfaction is unparalleled. The game also has a robust multiplayer component, which allows me to play with friends or other players from around the world, making each playthrough a new and exciting experience.

Of course, like any game, EU4 has its flaws. The game's AI can sometimes be unpredictable, leading to frustrating situations where the player's best-laid plans fall apart due to unexpected actions from the AI. Additionally, the game's interface can be overwhelming for new players, and the sheer amount of information presented on the screen can be intimidating at first.

Overall, EU4 is a game that has captured my heart and mind like no other. Its depth and historical accuracy, combined with its challenging gameplay and multiplayer component, make it a must-play for anyone who loves strategy games and is interested in exploring the intricacies of history.

There are three types of games. First there are those that are quick and easy to pick up, like card games. Secondly those that require a set-up, like Colonists of Catan or Monopoly. And lastly there are games that require hours of preparation and strategizing. Europa Universalis IV is part of the latter.

The game is based on a real world board game. That real life version uses a variety of chips, cards and pieces. This translates perfectly into a game version. But that also means that the game can become way more complicated as it is possible to code and track multiple features in the background. This is no turn based game. A day passes every couple of seconds and you can adjust the speed. The game uses different forms of currency or mana, like ducats, 'monarch power', manpower, sailors etc. These get updated every month, according to how you build your state.

[i]Setting[/i]
In Europa Universalis 4 (Eu4) you choose a nation in the year 1444. It is possible to select an exact date between 1444 and 1821, but it is advised to start in 1444. In this time frame the world changed drastically and you have to guide your country in becoming a prosperous and strong state. The game uses a historical time frame, but after unpausing the game for the first time, the game is completely ahistoric. It is up to the player to decide what to do.

[i]Gameplay[/i]
A core mechanic in Eu4 is strategically using your 'mana'. Everything has a cost. Integrating vasals, coring new land, recruiting generals, developing your land etc. uses monarch power. (administrative, diplomatic and militairy) The amount of monarch power you gain depends mainly on your ruler's stats (0-0-0 to 6-6-6), your advisors and some other factors. There are more pools of mana like ducats and manpower. The gameplay loop is acquiring and using these pools. Becoming a good player means knowing how to balance your mana usage and how to get even more mana.

[i]DLC's[/i]
Eu4 has a lot of 'DLC's'. Some give flavour to a region or play style. Others add core mechanics and there are also skins and sound tracks available. As a new player it's difficult to grasp this insane list of add-ons. Eu4 gets an update every half-year to a year. There is a free part of the update and a DLC part. This is how Eu4 is monetized.
I advise that you [b]ONLY[/b] buy Eu4 on sale and try it out. Learn the core mechanics. Try a big country around Europe, like France, the Ottomans, England, Spain or Poland. Watch video's on YouTube, read stuff on the wiki and look at achievements and formeable nations. You will find an obstacle in the form of a missing DLC. Decide if it's worth to buy necessary DLC's (and wait for big sales, like on Instant Gaming). This requires a lot of strategizing, in game and when buying DLC's. At least if you want to think economically. Remember, Eu4 is the acquivalent of a Warhammer board game. You need to buy trinkets and extra's to play the game. 
--> Read the wiki for more information on DLC's, but here is a quick summary:

[i]DLC help[/i]
[i]Conquest of Paradise:[/i] If you want to play in the New World
[i]Wealth of Nations:[/i] Core mechanics for trade
[i]Res Publica:[/i] Core mechanics for republics and mana
[i]Art of War:[/i] Core mechanics for diplomacy like vassals (+ religion wars and Napoleonic wars)
[i]El Dorado:[/i] Better Conquest of Paradise, cool custom nation designer.
[i]Common Sense:[/i] Core mechanic for government, flavour for parliaments and some religions
[i]The Cossacks:[/i] Core mechanics for Hordes and cool features
[i]Mare Nostrum:[/i] Extra cool features, should be in base game
[i]Rights of Man:[/i] Lots of quality of life improvements
[i]Mandate of Heaven:[/i] Flavour for Eastern Asia (China, Japan) Quality of life + Cool extra's like Historical Ages
[i]Cradle of Civilization:[/i] Flavour for Middle East + Core mechanics that should be in base game
[i]Dharma:[/i] Flavour for India + Core mechanics that should be in base game (trade company, government reforms)
[i]Emperor:[/i] Flavour for Europe + extra's for late game
[i]Leviathan:[/i] Flavour for South-Eastern Asia and Oceania + Monuments (I bought this game only for the monuments)
[i]Third Rome:[/i] Flavour for Eastern Europe and mostly Russia
[i]Rule Britannia:[/i] Flavour for the English isles + core mechanics for the navy, innovation and Industrial Revolution

[i]DLC controversy[/i]
Eu4 is monetized with DLC's. But a quick glance on the summary I gave shows the general disgust. Flavour for certain regions is nice, but a single or a couple of core mechanics are put behind a paywall. Sometimes you even need an older DLC to experience a newer DLC. Lions of the North adds more monuments. But you need Leviathan to unlock the monuments mechanic!
[i]Leviathan debacle[/i]
In 2020 1.30 Emperor was released. It was a buggy mess but the devs fixed it within a month. A year later 1.31 Leviathan released. This DLC and update broke the game and netted the worst reviewed DLC of all time on Steam. Lots of players quit or refused to play 1.31. I myself stayed on 1.30 untill 2022. After that a new team took over Eu4. They released 1.32 Origins. Which is a good flavour DLC without significant paywall mechanics. There was a very good free update 1.33 that made the AI actually competent and late 2022 they released the well received 1.34 Lions of the North, again without big core mechanics behind paywalls. Hopefully the trend continues. Eu4 is in a healthy position and can still offer a lot of fun. But there is a lot of potential in the form of mods. The Fantasy Total Conversion Mod: Anbennar might even be considered its own title as it's a complete different experience.

I have written this review to negate some of the unfair reviews that give this game a negative score. I do admit the last couple of dlcs have been lackluster (Mare Nostrum, and The Cossacks specifically), however if the dlcs are not giving enough content for their price do not buy it. It is your choice if you decided to pay fifteen dollars for a lackluster dlc and the opinon of the dlc should not be the determination for the base game's score. There are many excellent expanions released for eu4, that in my opinon would negate any negativity from the last two expansions .

The base game in itself is a game that I would reccomend playing. I have played many hours in vanilla itself. The game is a grand strategey with much more depth than games like the civ series. You play a nation of your choosing, and attempt to do as best as you can with it. Some nations are easier than other due to this game being based on history ( France is stronger than a Native American nation). The game is like a puzzle, many hours will be spent figuring out alliances, truces, aggressive expansion opinon modifiers, religion to be able to conquer the world without destroying yourself in the process. There are national ideas and events which make many nations unique in their playstyle, and there are idea groups which you unlock which give you various bonuses that can further specalize your nation. One thing that is amazing about this game is whenever something happens that could ruin my game it is always my fault, and it is something that you can learn from and choose to never make the same mistake again.

The DLC is one thing that is essential to review, there are a lot of dlc for this game. Don't judge the game on the the price of every dlc combined, many DLC are just cosmetic and music addition packs. There are a few dlcs that are expansions to the game ( Res Publica, Wealth of Nations, Conquest of Paradise, Art of War, and Common Sense) which in my opinon are all essential and worth every penny spent on them. If you are scared of the hefty base price of these dlc combined, don't be scared as they frequently go for sale up to 75% off, so you can get all these expansions for less than 10 dollars if you wait for good sales. If you wait long enough the recent dlc (Cossacks and Mare Nostrum) will probably be given huge sales as well.

I would not reccomend this game who are looking for quick fun, this is a game you sit down for hours at a time to plan and fail, and then restart the game over, and then fail but do a little better, then fail fail fail, and then you may finally perfect your game and do way better. A single playthrough can take around two weeks to get through, while it may take a lot of time it is really satisfying when all goes to plan and you acheive your goals. I would reccomend this to people who enjoyed civ games but are unsatisfied by the lack of depth or strategey in those games, I would reccomend this to people to have enjoyed playing Risk. In fact I reccomend this to most people I have met.

This game is good; fantastic, in fact. It's my most played game of all time and the first I've gotten to over one thousand hours, and I'm sure I'll continue to play it for at least a few hundred more. However, I absolutely cannot recommend paying over $200 for this game. 

Speaking generally, EUIV has seen the following happen:

-Game releases in a solid-ish state, but lacking some mechanical depth

-First few DLCs are fairly content rich (if mildly overpiced), and after three or four, the game reaches a much better state

-Despite already effectively doubling the price, DLC rarely goes down in price significantly enough to bring the full game to allow new players entry without breaking the bank

-DLC continues to get added, but Paradox begins seemingly running out of ideas/ability to push the game further, leading to one or two major improvements per expansion without a corresponding decrease in cost

-Now, over half a decade after release, the full EUIV experience can only be experienced for hundreds of dollars

At this stage, I think entering the game as a new player is far too expensive to justify the product, especially for someone new to the genre. EUIV is a game with a tremendous mechanical depth and variety, meaning that it takes two hours at least to locate all the buttons you can use. Steam's refund policy makes experimenting to see if you enjoy EUIV next to impossible. Unless Paradox makes significant changes to their DLC pricing, you should absolutely wait for Europa Universalis V and pray they don't screw it up like they did for Imperator: Rome.

Europa Universalis IV is a game focused around war, trade, and exploration.  What it really excels in is war, the other two 'focuses' of the game have been improved over time, but the game still revolves around war.  This wouldn't be a problem if with every patch they wouldn't make conquest more tedious.  From the 1.7 to the 1.8 patch (Art of War, released in November 2014), conquest was made much, much easier, and completing World Conquests (A particular feat, being the only independent nation left in the world) was made much easier.  From there, Paradox has been adding roadblock after roadblock to conquest.  This is okay, though.  If conquest was as easy as point and click, and no thought has to be put into it, then this game wouldn't be such an engaging, addicting, and fun experience.

This game's learning curve is interesting.  I can't remember much of my early experience but you're given a complex yet simple interface, tooltips that don't mean much (which has been helped with some semi-recent patches), tutorials that also don't help much, and, of course, the shock of "What am I supposed to do?  Is there a goal?"  The answer to those questions is both simple and intimidating, and it slaps you in the face rather abruptly.  It depends.  You do whatever it is you like, there is a score system but it doesn't really mean much.  That means that short of being in 1st place at the end of the game (which is rather easy for most nations), there is no goal.  You take control of your nation, you embody it.  That nation is you.  It took me about 4-6 hours to understand how to play the game, and another ~100 to 'git good'.  I stopped improving as a player (much) at about 1500 hours.

In short, this game is about entering the renaissance, takes a huge time investment, is super fun, and hard to learn.

This game came out almost 5 years ago and the developers are constantly releasing new and exciting content to keep me engaged through various playthroughs. There is often a great deal of concern about the "DLC Policy" of the game and while it may be incredibly daunting to pick up this game and realize their is over $200 worth of additional content it is often misrepresented in what is actually required to play the game. The base game itself is perfectly capable of being played alone,

While the base game is good, each DLC adds some really neat content that makes the game that much more enjoyable, especially in certain regions of the world, the most commonly highest rated among the DLC are, Art of War, Common Sense, and Rights of Man.

((Scroll to bottom for overall rankings))

Starting in chronological order,

Conquest of Paradise: One of the most commonly skipped DLC among players who do not play as major colonial powers or as native american nations. Most prominent feature being the random new world, this one is one I would pass on at first.

Wealth of Nations: Another largely skippable expansion, those who enjoy the trading aspects of the game can pick up more from trade capitals, piracy, trade conflicts, and trade companies. Also helped flesh out the Reformed religion. Most prominent feature being Trade companies for overseas trade generation.

Res Publica: This one is the Low Countries DLC it focused mainly on the areas of the Netherlands and added changes for republics throughout Europe. Most important feature for overall gameplay is ability to focus on one monarch point at the expense of the other two.

Art of War: Vastly changes the war gameplay of the game, new late game empire management, pushing of subject cb, rebel support, and allied war mechanics. Most prominent feature, the ability to transfer occupation of a province from one war ally to another.

El Dorado: Another New World expansion, El Dorado focuses on Latin America and new world exploration. Colonial players will like this one given gold fleets, and exploration mechanics. Most prominent feature: Custom Nation Designer

Common Sense: One of the core expansions designed to help develop your own nation, completely changes the way of improving provinces by expending monarch points to improve base tax, productivity, or manpower.  Improved government options for England. Most Prominent Feature: Provincial Improvement

The Cossacks: Micromanaging land and factions within your country via estates can be really rewarding. Also adds incredible depth to Horde nations throughout the game, (Golden Horde, Kazan, all the way out to Qing etc) Most Important feature: Estates Management

Mare Nostrum: Often considered one of the weaker expansions Mare Nostrum creates new missions for the automation of naval fleets, expands N. African raiding, some minor tweeks to espionage and for Merchant Republics the ability to create Trade Leagues. The most prominent feature however, is the ability to rent out your army through the new Condottieri system.

Rights of Man: Large nations benefit most from Rights of Man via the great power system allowing for some very powerful diplomatic interactions. Rulers generate traits for more depth, and Queens can serve as Regent to prevent regency councils in the case of underage rulers. Vassals work better through targeted goals and most of non Muslim Africa gains more religious depth (Fetishist and Coptic) Most Prominent Feature: Ruler Personalities and Queen/King Consorts.

Mandate of Heaven: For those who like to play in the Far East this is one of the most important you can play as. Tributary system protects you from large western powers, while allowing you to grow. Ming has new control over their Empire, and Japan gains new rule sets regarding their Daimos. Most prominent feature: Historical Ages/Golden Era. Each Game is divided into 4 subsections where completing age goals can unlock powerful bonuses during that time.

Third Rome: This one really isn't a full expansion pack, it's what they call an Immersion Pack. The pack itself adds a great deal of cosmetic unit models and fleshes out the governments of those in the Russia region. The Orthodoxy also gains a great deal of depth. Most prominent feature being Russian Governments

Cradle of Civilization: The most recent expansion, Cradle of Civilization adds some new trade policies for merchants, more depth to Islam, the ability to sacrifice a province development for short term gains and Army professionalism. The most prominent ability is the ability to develop your army through the game to give bonuses to their performance in combat, and bonuses to your overall countries capabilities in war. Most prominent feature: Army Professionalism/Drilling

Coming Soon: Rule Brittania, have not played this one yet, but it completely redesigns the mission system allowing for more powerful rewards and more scripted gameplay. Large changes to the British Isles and the Low countries in development, religion, and unit packs. Finally those who push tech and build tall will be rewarded through the new innovativeness mechanic.

Recommendations:

Must have: Rights of Man, Art of War, Common Sense
Next in Line: The Cossacks, Res Publica
Situational: Mandate of Heaven (Far East), Cradle of Civilization (Islam), Conquest of Paradise (New World), El Dorado (Colonial), Wealth of Nations (Trade Leagues), Mare Nostrum (Naval Power or Proxy War)
Only if: Third Rome (Ottomans or Russian Region), Rule Brittania (Any British Nation or Dutch)

Please note, the developer Paradox Interactive frequently offers sales for this product and older DLC. While I consider the base game and the Must Have's as being worth full price, the others you can pick up at discounts up to 75% off through a sale.

You might be better off never setting your foot into this game in the first place. If you are browsing the store now, you might be too late for the show. I'll explain why I think of it this way.

Released in 2013, 6 years ago as of writing this, the game has been continuously developing and evolving, which per se is great.
The current game is vastly different from what it was many years ago.
It can be said that with the DLCs and patches, at some point along the journey the game became EU5, then with more DLC and changes it became EU6.
However, instead of releasing an entirely new next game, they've continuously pumped out patches and DLCs and piled them on top of the existing game.

Now the current game with all its features behind DLC is about $450 CAD. In a sense EU4 was 50 ish bucks 6 years ago, now the EU4 with updated features but without DLC content is still 50 ish bucks (which is still more like EU5). With all the DLC contents, which turns the game into more of a EU6 is $450.

Chances are, you'll be hard split between spending hundreds of dollars in a single game, which you may or may not enjoy for 2000 hours or so, and spending that money you can buy perhaps 8 to 10 other games that may give you more variety and hours.

Often the recommendation is to buy the DLCs are on sale, but other games go on sale as well. This made it very difficult for me to choose the DLCs to extend the life of this game for me and miss out on other games. Unless you spend enough money to do both, you'd probably experience this issue as well.

That said, newer players and the casuals like me would never get to experience the latest EU4, the latest version became unreasonable to attain.

So if you for some reason decide to buy this game with DLCs omitted, know that that's probably where you'd stay.
I've realized that at some point I've stopped watching youtube videos or reading posts about EU4. What I had was no longer same as what those dedicated core fans played. I was playing EU5, they were playing EU6 or 7.

Rants about the DLC costs are constant and abundant here and I'm sure others are tired of seeing another one.
Again, yes, the game itself is fun to the point of being addictive, even without all the DLCs. However, this is not a pointless whine.

If you are fine with that, go ahead and purchase the game. However, know that you'll always be aware of the features locked behind the DLC and the latest and the fullest game would be $450 or more as additional DLCs get released. Also, keep in mind that with the same amount of money you can probably buy up to 10 or 12 other games with great reviews.

That said, with all this headache, even after admitting that even the base game is great, my recommendation is to not set your foot into this franchise at this point. The ship has sailed too far out to the sea. At the very least try the "Extreme edition" (which no longer became fitting of "extreme") and see if you want to spend more money on a single game instead of buying another full game.

Had the developers stopped releasing patches and DLCs and wrapped up EU4 at some point and released "EU5", it may have been easier for the newcomers to get the full game. In a sense, the newcomers are forced to buy all the previous versions in order to get the full game. This multi-year ongoing development and trails of DLC style of system is great for the old fans, but not for the newcomers.

Europa Universalis IV, a grand strategy game by Paradox Interactive, is an intricate and expansive look at world history from 1444 to 1821. As a novice casual gamer, I found myself both overwhelmed and fascinated by the depth of the gameplay. This game isn’t your typical pick-up-and-play; it demands attention to detail and a lot of patience.

When you first start the game, the learning curve can feel steep. You're presented with a map of the world filled with various nations, each with their own goals and challenges. As a player, you can choose any nation, from major empires like France or England to smaller states like Saxony or Navarre. The game's complexity comes from managing aspects of your nation such as diplomacy, trade, warfare, and internal administration.

What struck me was how each decision I made had far-reaching consequences, affecting not just my nation but also my relationships with neighbours and global powers. The game's depth in terms of diplomacy and conflict strategies is impressive. You can engage in espionage, form coalitions, declare trade wars, or even support rebels in foreign lands. However, for a casual player, managing these intricate aspects simultaneously can be daunting.

The game shines in its historical accuracy and attention to detail. The events and characters reflect real historical figures and scenarios, which adds an educational layer to the experience. However, without a strong interest in history or strategy, the appeal might not be as strong for all casual gamers.

Graphically, the game is quite functional but not particularly stunning, which is typical for strategy games that emphasise mechanics over visuals. The user interface is packed with information, and while it is effective, it can be intimidating for new players.

In conclusion, Europa Universalis IV is a rewarding game for those willing to invest the time to learn its mechanics. For a casual gamer like myself, it presents a significant challenge and a steep learning curve but also offers a uniquely satisfying experience when you finally steer your nation to prosperity and victory. It’s not for everyone, but if you have a keen interest in history and strategic planning, this game might just captivate you as it did me.
